strengths: Novel problem formulation combining synthesizable 2D generation with 3D structure generation, addressing a genuine gap in the field
Substantial dataset contribution (SYNSPACE) with 622,766 molecules and 3.36M conformers using building block reaction graphs rather than synthons
Technically sound methodology with clever solutions (visibility-aware coordinate masking in Algorithm 1, unified time diffusion, training-time constraints)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple orthogonal metrics, proper baselines, and thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art 3D generation while significantly outperforming on synthesizability (96.7% validity, 50-72% retrosynthesis solve rate)
Practical demonstration of utility through molecular inpainting where valid molecules achieve 58-79% retrosynthetic solve rate vs. 0% for DiffLinker
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and logical narrative structure
Excellent analysis of conformer quality through distribution matching of bond geometries and energies
weaknesses: Limited chemical diversity with intentionally constrained vocabulary (93 building blocks, 19 reactions) that significantly restricts chemical space and may limit practical applicability to real drug discovery

Equivariance violation (acknowledged but not adequately addressed): coordinate masking scheme breaks SE(3) equivariance, and positional embeddings intentionally break permutation invariance of base architecture

Limited real-world validation of synthesizability claims: molecules procedurally generated rather than experimentally validated; retrosynthesis solver success rates (~50-70% on known drugs) limit confidence in 50-72% SYNCOGEN scores

Experimental comparison fairness issues: different baselines trained for different epochs (MiDi/EQGAT-diff up to 800 vs SYNCOGEN 100), only SemlaFlow retrained on SYNSPACE, retrosynthesis evaluated on only 100 samples
Conformer generation underperforms baseline: 61.4% coverage vs. 69.2% ETKDG on simpler task with limited analysis of failure modes
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices without sensitivity analysis: loss weights (0.4, 0.4, 0.2), noise scaling coefficient (0.2), time threshold (0.25) all lack justification
Missing critical ablation: no evidence that building-block constraint improves synthesizability vs. generating freely and filtering by retrosynthesis solvers
Fragment linking called 'zero-shot' but uses trained vocabulary; limited to 3 protein targets and produces fewer valid molecules (46.9-57.6%) than baselines despite claims of utility
Reproducibility concerns: missing URLs for code/data (marked as '.'), train/test split details not described, incomplete hyperparameter documentation
Incomplete comparisons: other reaction-based methods (RGFN, SynFlowNet) cited but not benchmarked; no comparison with other 3D inpainting approaches; no drug-likeness analysis (Lipinski's rules)

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach addressing the practical problem of ensuring synthesizability in 3D molecular generation through building-block-aware joint generation of graphs and coordinates

Strong empirical results with state-of-the-art performance on unconditional generation (96.7% validity, competitive retrosynthesis validity) and demonstrated advantages on conditional generation tasks

Comprehensive experimental validation including multiple baselines, extensive ablations, diverse evaluation metrics, and practical applications in drug discovery (fragment linking, pharmacophore-conditioned generation)
Valuable dataset contribution (SynSPACE) with 1.2M molecules combining real synthesis constraints and 7.5M conformations
Detailed technical description with clear algorithms, thorough hyperparameter specification, and commitment to code release enabling reproducibility
Sophisticated training-time constraints that enforce chemical validity (compatibility masking, edge constraints) without requiring external reward models
weaknesses: Limited component-level technical novelty - masked graph diffusion and flow matching are adapted from prior work, with the main contribution being their combination for synthesis-aware generation
Experimental validation of actual synthesizability is entirely computational; fragment linking tested on only 3 PDB structures limits scope; no comparison with dedicated retrosynthesis software tools

Building block vocabulary is restricted (93 core blocks), potentially limiting the chemical design space and generalization beyond drug-like molecules to other chemical classes (materials, polymers, etc.)
Insufficient analysis of failure modes, out-of-distribution performance, or sensitivity to building block set composition; unclear how the approach generalizes to novel chemistry
Computational efficiency not thoroughly addressed - multi-step sampling procedure and resource requirements (2 H100 GPUs) not compared against baselines in terms of inference time
Heavy reliance on computational proxies for retrosynthesis validation; actual retrosynthesis solve rates (50-72%) suggest room for improvement in practical applicability
